A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world each placement lands at the left-right mirror of the chosen anchor: a brick dx cells wide chosen at column x lands at column 8 - dx - x, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds. With the default recipe it gets only 131k steps, which is 32 updates. That looks too few for an exact build. A placement is safe only if it lands at the lowest missing layer of every column under it. The footprint max/min pooling heads already suit that check, but the starting net has to discover per-layer landing logic from columns mixed together. Round 1 separates two possible causes. First, recipe: fewer PPO epochs buy 1.9× to 3.3× more samples and more updates. Candidates A and C put the starting net on the same recipe and differ only in epochs (2 vs 1). Second, architecture: B scores each placement separately for each landing layer, then combines the layer scores with a logsumexp. B uses A's recipe, so comparing B with A shows the effect of the architecture alone.

### Round 2
All three trials scored exactly 0 on dev and also 0 on training success. They used two quite different aligned designs (the baseline, and a per-layer landing scorer that builds in the drop logic) and three recipes (4, 2 and 1 PPO epochs). Seed noise can't explain a result that is zero everywhere, so the failure is systematic. Both architectures assume that action index (t, y, x) lines up spatially with observation cell (y, x), because they produce placement logits with convolutions and footprint pooling. The task warns that the world may differ from its description. If the action indexing is transposed, flipped or offset relative to the observation, or the footprints differ, a convolutional head can't learn the remapping, and both designs would fail in exactly this way. Wall time is far from binding (about 80 s). FLOPs are binding, and a network below r=1 gets no extra samples. This round tests heads that don't assume alignment.

### Round 3
All six trials score exactly 0 on dev and in training, including the last 10% of training. The three recipes (1, 2 and 4 epochs), the per-layer landing head and the unaligned MLP heads all fail the same way. Seed noise cannot explain this. Even a weak shaped policy should sometimes finish 6-brick designs, so learning is probably broken, not just slow. Two causes are likely. First, the hard-coded footprint pooling may not match the world: footprint orientation or anchor convention may differ, or actions may be indexed transposed. Second, there may be too few policy updates. The flat MLP heads might fix the first problem but learn too slowly. So the next tests use a local head that is free of convention assumptions: a learned 3x3 conv per brick type, with coordinate channels. I add an optional path that handles transposed indexing, and I separately test many small updates.

### Round 4
All nine trials scored exactly 0 on dev, and 0 on training success in the last 10% too, across every seed. Three kinds of change made no difference: recipes (1, 2 or 4 epochs; 74 to 300 updates), heads (footprint pooling, a free conv head, a transposed head, a global MLP head) and per-layer structure. Trials took 30 to 180 s, far below the 900 s limit, so time is not the constraint. Since the networks differ so much and all score 0, I suspect a mismatch in the world rather than slow learning. One candidate is a global spatial misalignment, for example the target shown permuted or shifted relative to the build or the actions. Local convolutions cannot learn that. The flat MLP head could, but it is data-hungry. For this last round I test three ways to mix information globally while keeping weights shared across cells: an MLP-Mixer, a conv network with learned cell-to-cell mixing, and a transformer with learned positions. Any score above 0 would be selected.
